title: Ezekiel 34:11–24
context: The LORD declares, “Behold, I myself, even I, will search for my sheep, and will seek them out” (34:11). He will gather them from the countries, bring them into their own land, and feed them on the mountains of Israel (34:12–14): “I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep” (34:15). He will do what the failed shepherds did not, seeking the lost and binding up the broken, while he will “destroy the fat and the strong” (34:16). The LORD then turns to the flock itself: “I judge between sheep and sheep,” between the fat sheep who trample the pasture and foul the water and the lean sheep they push aside (34:17–22). Finally the LORD promises, “I will set up one shepherd over them,” “even my servant David”, and “my servant David prince among them” (34:23–24). The historical David had long been dead, so the promise is commonly read as pointing to a ruler from David’s line, in keeping with the covenant of 2 Samuel 7, which both traditions treat as shared ground; compare 37:24–25. Christian readers in both traditions commonly see the promise fulfilled in Christ, the good shepherd of John 10:11, while reading it first in its own setting.

verses.text: “ ‘For the Lord GOD says: “Behold, I myself, even I, will search for my sheep, and will seek them out.
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, I myself, even I, will search for my sheep, and will seek them out.” Arminian readers note the LORD’s personal initiative in seeking the lost, and they see in it a love that goes out to the scattered and calls them home.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD taking the work of seeking into his own hands, and many stress that his seeking is effective in finding his own. Shared ground: both traditions read the emphatic “I myself, even I” as the heart of the chapter: where human shepherds failed, the LORD himself acts.

verses.text: As a shepherd seeks out his flock in the day that he is among his sheep that are scattered abroad, so I will seek out my sheep. I will deliver them out of all places where they have been scattered in the cloudy and dark day.
verses.arminianNotes: “As a shepherd seeks out his flock”, the LORD will “deliver them out of all places where they have been scattered in the cloudy and dark day.” Arminian readers note the tenderness of the image and the hope it gives to exiles who felt abandoned.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s faithful care reaching his people wherever they have been driven. Shared ground: both traditions read “the cloudy and dark day” as the day of judgment and exile, and both see the promise of rescue as pure mercy.

verses.text: I will bring them out from the peoples, and gather them from the countries, and will bring them into their own land. I will feed them on the mountains of Israel, by the watercourses, and in all the inhabited places of the country.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will bring them out from the peoples, and gather them from the countries, and will bring them into their own land.” Arminian readers note the promise of return from exile, given to a people who had just heard of the city’s fall.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD keeping his covenant promises of the land despite the people’s unfaithfulness. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse first as a promise of return from exile, and many in both also see it pointing toward a fuller gathering of God’s people.

verses.text: I will feed them with good pasture, and their fold will be on the mountains of the height of Israel. There they will lie down in a good fold. They will feed on rich pasture on the mountains of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will feed them with good pasture,” and “There they will lie down in a good fold.” Arminian readers note the picture of rest and abundance after scattering. The LORD provides what the false shepherds withheld.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s provision as complete and generous, recalling the shepherd imagery of Psalm 23. Shared ground: both traditions read the “good pasture” and “rich pasture” as images of the LORD’s care, without forcing a doctrinal fork from them.

verses.text: I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep, and I will cause them to lie down,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes: “I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep, and I will cause them to lie down,” says the Lord GOD. Arminian readers note the LORD’s direct and personal care, a promise both comforting and humbling to those who had trusted in human leaders.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD claiming the shepherd’s role for himself. Shared ground: both traditions hold this together with the promise of a Davidic shepherd in 34:23, reading the LORD’s own shepherding and the shepherd he sets up as belonging together.

verses.text: “I will seek that which was lost, and will bring back that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick; but I will destroy the fat and the strong. I will feed them in justice.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: “I will seek that which was lost, and will bring back that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken”. Arminian readers note that the LORD does exactly what 34:4 said the shepherds failed to do. Yet he will “destroy the fat and the strong”, so his care is joined to justice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD reversing the shepherds’ neglect point by point, and they note the closing words, “I will feed them in justice.” Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as joining mercy to the weak with judgment on oppressors, and many hear it echoed in Luke 19:10.

verses.text: “As for you, O my flock, the Lord GOD says: ‘Behold, I judge between sheep and sheep, the rams and the male goats.
verses.arminianNotes: “As for you, O my flock,” the LORD says, “I judge between sheep and sheep, the rams and the male goats.” Arminian readers note that the LORD now turns from the shepherds to the flock itself. Accountability reaches every member, not only the leaders.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see judgment within the flock, as the LORD distinguishes among his people. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that the people are not merely victims of bad rulers; the strong among them also wronged the weak. Some readers compare Matthew 25:32–33, each in its own setting.

verses.text: Does it seem a small thing to you to have fed on the good pasture, but you must tread down with your feet the residue of your pasture? And to have drunk of the clear waters, but must you foul the residue with your feet?
verses.arminianNotes: The strong sheep “fed on the good pasture,” yet “tread down with your feet the residue”, and foul the clear waters. Arminian readers note the selfishness that spoils what others need. It is not enough to enjoy one’s own share; the strong must not ruin the rest.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the image as exposing greed and contempt for the weak within the community. Shared ground: both traditions read the trampling and fouling as concrete pictures of injustice among God’s people, and both apply them to how the strong treat the vulnerable.

verses.text: As for my sheep, they eat that which you have trodden with your feet, and they drink that which you have fouled with your feet.’
verses.arminianNotes: “As for my sheep, they eat that which you have trodden with your feet”. Arminian readers note that the LORD again calls the weak “my sheep,” taking up their cause against those who have spoiled their food and water.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD identifying with the oppressed within his flock. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that the LORD notices the harm done to the weakest, and that he counts it as done to his own sheep.

verses.text: “Therefore the Lord GOD says to them: ‘Behold, I, even I, will judge between the fat sheep and the lean sheep.
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, I, even I, will judge between the fat sheep and the lean sheep.” Arminian readers note that the same emphatic “I, even I” that introduced the LORD’s searching in 34:11 now introduces his judging. Care and justice come from the same shepherd.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD as the one judge of his flock, whose judgment is part of his shepherding. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as promising that the lean will be vindicated and the fat held to account.

verses.text: Because you thrust with side and with shoulder, and push all the diseased with your horns, until you have scattered them abroad,
verses.arminianNotes: “you thrust with side and with shoulder, and push all the diseased with your horns, until you have scattered them abroad”. Arminian readers note that some of the scattering came from within the flock, as the strong drove out the weak.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the strong members of the community sharing the blame with the false shepherds. Shared ground: both traditions read the image soberly, as a charge against those who use strength to push others aside.

verses.text: therefore I will save my flock, and they will no more be a prey. I will judge between sheep and sheep.
verses.arminianNotes: “therefore I will save my flock, and they will no more be a prey. I will judge between sheep and sheep.” Arminian readers note that the LORD’s judgment serves his saving purpose: he judges in order to rescue the weak.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see salvation and judgment held together, as the LORD saves his flock by judging within it. Shared ground: both traditions read “I will save my flock” as the LORD’s own promise of rescue, and both see it fulfilled in his care for the weak.

verses.text: I will set up one shepherd over them, and he will feed them, even my servant David. He will feed them, and he will be their shepherd.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will set up one shepherd over them, and he will feed them, even my servant David.” Christian readers in both traditions commonly see this fulfilled in Christ, the son of David. Arminian readers stress that the one shepherd feeds and gathers the flock, and compare John 10:11 in passing. Since the historical David had long been dead, a Davidic ruler is meant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise commonly read the promise messianically, rooted in the covenant with David in 2 Samuel 7, which both traditions treat as shared ground. Shared ground: both note that the historical David was long dead, so the promise points to a ruler from his line, and both compare 37:24–25 and John 10:11 while reading the verse first in its own setting.

verses.text: I, the LORD, will be their God, and my servant David prince among them. I, the LORD, have spoken it.
verses.arminianNotes: “I, the LORD, will be their God, and my servant David prince among them.” Arminian readers note that the LORD’s covenant relationship with his people and the rule of his servant David belong together. The covenant formula frames the promise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the Davidic prince ruling under the LORD, not in place of him, and many read the verse as fulfilled in Christ. Shared ground: both traditions read “prince” with 37:25 and 2 Samuel 7, and both hold the messianic reading with the humility appropriate to prophecy.
